title: Investing: Tax changes accelerate rotation to value stocks
full_text:
For the best part of a decade, Australian growth stocks trounced their value counterparts as low interest rates in the 2010s boosted the value of their future earnings. But value investors now believe their corner of the market is in the midst of a resurgence, which could be turbocharged by tax changes announced in the federal budget.
Investors started rotating into value stocks - those that are inexpensive relative to their earnings - as Australia emerged from the pandemic, when the Reserve Bank aggressively increased interest rates to contain inflation. The trade has been turbocharged over the past year as the RBA lifted rates in response to the spike in energy prices caused by the Iran war.
The S&P/ASX 200 value index rallied 20.2 per cent in the 2025-26 financial year, beating the Australian growth index by more than 25 per cent - the largest outperformance in over 16 years, according to S&P Dow Jones Indices. Value has also outperformed growth by roughly 53 per cent on a cumulative basis over the five years to June 30.
"From a fundamental perspective, growth stocks rely on a more rosy outlook, so if people are nervous about the economy or whatever is going on locally, it's less likely they will be willing to attribute a high multiple for future earnings," said Michael Goldberg, portfolio manager of the Collins St Value Fund.
"In a risk-off environment, it's much easier to attribute a value to current earnings than trying to predict what future earnings look like, which is why growth stocks are struggling."
While value investors seek out companies trading below their full potential, growth investors look for businesses with stronger earnings growth prospects, such as tech stocks.
When deciding which shares should be included in the ASX 200 growth index, S&P Dow Jones looks at metrics like three-year earnings per share growth rates and momentum - the 12-month change in a share price. For its value index, it considers factors like a stock's earnings-to-price ratio and sales-to-price ratio.
That means the sector composition of each index can shift over time to reflect changes in share prices as well as sales and earnings growth of underlying companies. Rising valuations among the large banks have increased financials' representation in the ASX 200 growth index, which now includes Commonwealth Bank.
By contrast, the ASX 200 value index is below its long-term average weight in financials and above its long-term average weight in materials. That has boosted the performance of the index, given the huge rally in resources stocks over the past year.
The proposed changes to capital gains tax announced in the federal budget have further enhanced the appeal of value stocks, given that they are more likely to pay dividends. Growth stocks, on the other hand, typically reinvest any profits into expansion and innovation.
From next year, individuals selling assets such as shares and exchange-traded funds will pay tax on the total investment gain, adjusted for inflation. Under the current system, investors are only taxed on half of the gains, known as the 50 per cent discount.
Retail investors have piled into ETFs that are focused on dividends, bonds and cash since the changes were announced. Money flowing into cash and fixed-income-focused ETFs more than doubled in June to $1 billion from $494 million in May.
"In terms of the recent federal budget, we believe it further incentivises investing for profits and income rather than relying on future capital gains," said Reece Birtles, head of Australian equities at ClearBridge Investments. "Value and income-focused strategies are fundamentally centred on companies generating enduring profits and distributing income to shareholders each year."
Local growth funds, which hunt for companies expected to grow their sales and earnings at a significantly faster rate than the broader market, were already among the biggest laggards.
Hyperion Asset Management's Small Growth Companies Fund sank 34.3 per cent in the 12 months to June 30, making it the second-worst performing equity fund in Australia over that period, according to Fund Monitors. Hyperion's Australian Growth Companies Fund was the third worst, tumbling 29.2 per cent for the year.
ECP Asset Management's Growth Companies Fund was the fourth-worst, declining 27.9 per cent.
The horror year for the two high-profile fund managers was partly fuelled by the so-called SaaSpocalypse earlier this calendar year, when investors dumped software stocks over fears that artificial intelligence would disrupt their business.
Growth funds that invest in markets beyond Australia have held up far better given their exposure to Wall Street, where technology stocks continue to surge on the back of the artificial intelligence revolution. However, outside the US, value stocks have outperformed growth in many developed markets over the past five years, including Canada, Japan and Europe.
